title: Computing 'this year's birthday' for someone born on Feb 29 crashes in Python and silently becomes March 1 in JS
assumption: You can always construct 'this year's version' of someone's birthday by combining the current year with their birth month and day.

input.display: date(2023, 2, 29)  (constructing the 2023 birthday of someone born 2000-02-29, where 2023 is not a leap year)
input.description: Anniversary/birthday reminder features, age-at-next-birthday calculations, and loyalty-program 'birthday month' logic for anyone born on February 29.

what_goes_wrong: A 'days until your next birthday' feature for a Feb-29 user either crashes outright (Python) or silently reports their birthday as March 1st (JavaScript) in every year that isn't a leap year -- and the two backends disagree with each other about which day that is.
why: February 29 only exists in leap years. Python's `date()` constructor validates the day against the given year and raises `ValueError` for `date(2023, 2, 29)` because 2023 is not a leap year. JavaScript's `Date` constructor performs no such validation: field overflow silently rolls forward, so `new Date(2023, 1, 29)` (month index 1 = February) normalizes to March 1, 2023. Neither answer is 'the real February 29 of 2023' because there isn't one; the two runtimes just fail in opposite styles, loud versus silent.

repros.code:
from datetime import date

birth = date(2000, 2, 29)
reference_year = 2023  # not a leap year
try:
    this_years_birthday = date(reference_year, birth.month, birth.day)
    print("birthday:", this_years_birthday)
except ValueError as e:
    print("error constructing this year's birthday:", e)
repros.expected_output: error constructing this year's birthday: day 29 must be in range 1..28 for month 2 in year 2023

fix: Decide and document a policy for Feb-29 anniversaries in non-leap years (commonly Feb 28 or Mar 1) and apply it explicitly -- check `calendar.isleap(year)` first and substitute the chosen fallback day, rather than letting the date constructor decide by crashing or overflowing.
